title: Breathless on exertion and a near-faint in a 74-year-old (clinic)

patient.name: Gordon Ashby
patient.chiefComplaint: Breathlessness on exertion and a near-faint last week
patient.setting: Outpatient clinic, seated in a chair

persona.affect: Stoic and matter-of-fact; plays his symptoms down and puts everything down to age; softens and becomes quietly worried when talking about his wife
persona.speakingStyle: Short, plain answers; doesn’t elaborate unless asked; says things like ‘it’s nothing really’; no medical jargon
persona.worries: Only came because his wife insisted after last week’s funny turn; does not want an operation or a hospital stay, because he cares for his wife, who has mild dementia and can’t be left alone for long
persona.background: Retired carpenter, married fifty years; still makes furniture in his workshop for the grandchildren; used to walk the family dog every morning

doorSign.task: Mr. Ashby, 74, presents with breathlessness on exertion and a near-faint last week. Take a focused history, perform a focused cardiovascular and respiratory examination, then present your summary, differential diagnosis and initial plan.

doorInstructions.reasonForVisit: Breathlessness on exertion and a near-faint
doorInstructions.task: Take a focused history and perform a focused physical examination. Share your impressions with the patient before you leave. You will then write a post-encounter note.

history.openingStatement: My wife made me come, really. I get a bit puffed on the stairs these days, and last week I had a funny turn. I’m sure it’s just my age.

facts.answer: It’s crept up on me over the last six months or so. Slowly getting worse, I suppose.

expectedDifferential.rationale: The classic exertional triad (breathlessness, angina, presyncope) in a 74-year-old told of a murmur years ago. Harsh, late-peaking crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border and radiating to both carotids, soft single S2, slow-rising low-volume carotid pulse, sustained non-displaced apex and a narrow pulse pressure (114/88). Symptoms mean urgent echocardiography and cardiology referral (valve replacement is the treatment for symptomatic severe stenosis). Meanwhile: avoid strenuous exertion; advise him not to drive until he has been assessed, since he had exertional presyncope and drives his wife; and review the amlodipine, because vasodilators can drop the blood pressure across a fixed outflow obstruction and worsen presyncope.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Coronary artery disease with stable angina
expectedDifferential.rationale: Exertional chest tightness relieved by rest plus age, male sex, hypertension, high cholesterol and 30 pack-years. Commonly coexists with aortic stenosis (angiography is usually done before valve intervention), but it does not explain the murmur, soft S2 or carotid pulse.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Arrhythmia (e.g. complete heart block or ventricular tachycardia) causing presyncope
expectedDifferential.rationale: Exertional presyncope warrants an ECG and ambulatory monitoring. Regular pulse at 72 and no palpitations make it less likely, but calcific valve disease can involve the conduction system.

Same exertional symptoms and an ejection systolic murmur, but its murmur is usually loudest at the left sternal border, does not radiate to the carotids, and the carotid upstroke is brisk (sometimes bifid); no family history of sudden death.
Exertional breathlessness, but no orthopnea, PND, edema, raised JVP or crackles. Can follow untreated severe aortic stenosis.
Common cause of an ejection murmur in older adults, but it does not cause symptoms, the S2 is preserved and the carotid pulse is normal, unlike here.

differential.rationale: Exertional breathlessness, angina and presyncope in a 74-year-old with a murmur noted years ago; harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, soft single S2, slow-rising low-volume carotid pulse, sustained non-displaced apex and a narrow pulse pressure. Advise no driving until assessed, and review the amlodipine (a vasodilator).

Exertional chest tightness relieved by rest with several risk factors (age, male, hypertension, high cholesterol, ex-smoker); often coexists with aortic stenosis but does not explain the murmur or the carotid pulse.

differential.diagnosis: Arrhythmia (e.g. heart block or ventricular tachycardia)
differential.rationale: Exertional presyncope needs an ECG and rhythm monitoring; less likely with a regular pulse of 72 and no palpitations, but calcific valve disease can extend into the conduction system.

Also causes exertional breathlessness, angina, presyncope and an ejection murmur, but the murmur is usually loudest at the left sternal border without carotid radiation, the carotid upstroke is brisk, and there is no family history of sudden death.
Exertional breathlessness, but no orthopnea, PND, edema, raised JVP or crackles; it may develop as a consequence of untreated severe aortic stenosis.
